doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Freddie Hubbard's drive and the trumpet method book idea
summary: Prompted by a line on his website, Weiss recalls interviewing Hubbard for a trumpet method book and sums him up as talent plus harder work and a determination born of being told to sit over there.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I want to read something from your website regarding the Cookers. It said the Cookers embody the serious-as-death commitment that it took to thrive on the New York scene some four decades ago.
I like that. Did I say that?
I was going to ask you. Well —
I think maybe somebody put something I was trying to convey into better words than I could.

Bless their little soul whoever they were. But I mean there was a lot of that. I mean at some point me and Freddie — Freddie Hubbard always wanted me to publish the charts I wrote of his music. I said that’s a great idea, Freddie, and I’m happy to do that but do you know what would really make an impact and sell a lot of books and you know help the world is a Freddie Hubbard trumpet method book. And we sat down and we did a bunch of interviews. And at the end of it it was all a lot of fun and I learned a little bit. But at the end I was like I think I could write this book in one paragraph. You had a ton of natural talent and you tried harder than everybody else. You practiced harder, you were more dedicated and more determined than anybody else I ever knew. You know?

And what else? Try playing this. But that’s the essence I got from it. And a lot of it was a competitive nature I think. And I mean I also got that from reading some Sonny Rollins stuff and discussions with Freddie about Sonny Rollins. Freddie got to New York — and this is the other thing I mean — sometimes when we’re sitting somewhere waiting, the stories, I mean Billy Harper’s story of trying to sit in with Elvin Jones is painful. Because they just didn’t let anybody — you know you want to be part of this? You know? Go sit over there. Freddie Hubbard told me that, the first time he went to a jam session in the Bronx they were like, “Who are you? Go sit over there and wait.” And at the end of the night, “Oh we forgot all about — come back tomorrow.” “What are you doing here? Go sit over there.” You know? And that kind of stuff drove him. I mean you know he was determined, and that’s what I see I mean not only all the immense talent and all the immense work but a drive. Like nobody’s going to tell me to sit over there again.
